## Appendix D — The master build order (rebuild from blank)

To build the whole stack from nothing, in order. Each milestone is one chapter; finish its tests
green before the next. This is the table of contents as a *to-do list*.

```text
   FOUNDATIONS
   [ ]  1. Read a packet off the TUN device; parse the IPv4 header; identify ICMP/TCP/UDP.
   [ ]  2. Implement the Internet checksum (utils); verify IP headers; reply to ICMP echo (ping).

   OPENING A CONNECTION
   [ ]  3. Parse the TCP header; seq arithmetic (seq.rs); the passive + active three-way handshake;
           randomized ISN; build_packet + the TCP pseudo-header checksum.
   [ ]  4. Accept data in ESTABLISHED; advance RCV.NXT; ACK; deliver to the app.
   [ ]  5. Passive close: receive FIN, ACK it, tear down.

   RELIABILITY AND TEARDOWN
   [ ]  6. Non-blocking event loop; the retransmission queue; adaptive RTO (rtt.rs, RFC 6298); Karn.
   [ ]  7. Active close + the full four-way teardown; TIME_WAIT (2·MSL).
   [ ]  8. Flow control: track the peer's window; advertise our receive window.
   [ ]  9. Reassembly (reassembly.rs): buffer out-of-order data; deliver the contiguous run.

   CONGESTION, THE SOCKET CORE, RETRANSMISSION
   [ ] 10. Congestion control (congestion.rs): slow start, AIMD, fast retransmit/recovery (RFC 5681).
   [ ] 11. The socket-style API: write/take_received/poll_transmit + send buffer; a tiny HTTP/1.0 reply.
   [ ] 12. Retransmit control segments (SYN/SYN-ACK/FIN) with exponential RTO backoff.

   SENDER BEHAVIOR AND OPTIONS
   [ ] 13. Nagle's algorithm + the TCP_NODELAY escape hatch.
   [ ] 14. Zero-window probes (the persist timer).
   [ ] 15. The TCP options framework + MSS negotiation; segment outgoing data to the MSS.
   [ ] 16. Timestamps: per-ACK RTT measurement + PAWS (RFC 7323 §3–4).
   [ ] 17. Window scaling: widen SND.WND to 32 bits (RFC 7323 §2).
   [ ] 18. SACK: negotiate SACK-Permitted; emit blocks; retransmit only the holes (RFC 2018).

   COMPLETING THE STACK
   [ ] 19. Finish the state machine: distinct CLOSE_WAIT + half-close, data+FIN, deferred OOO FIN;
           RFC 5961 RST/SYN challenge ACKs; RFC 1337 (ignore RST in TIME_WAIT).
   [ ] 20. NewReno: partial-ACK recovery (recover variable) — multiple losses, no RTO stall (RFC 6582).
   [ ] 21. SACK loss recovery: pipe estimator + IsLost + NextSeg; repair all holes in one RTT (RFC 6675).
   [ ] 22. The socket API: blocking TcpListener/TcpStream over a PacketIo trait (loopback-tested);
           active half-close (recv in FIN_WAIT_2); keep-alive HTTP/1.1 with full header buffering.
   [ ] 23. Robustness: RFC 5961 §5 ACK acceptability; randomized challenge-ACK throttle
           (CVE-2016-5696); CLOSE_WAIT / FIN_WAIT_2 reaper timeouts.

   MODERN RECOVERY, CONGESTION CONTROL, AND SCALE
   [ ] 24. RACK-TLP: time-based loss detection + Tail Loss Probe (RFC 8985), on timestamps + SACK.
   [ ] 25. CUBIC: cubic-in-time congestion avoidance for fat pipes, β = 0.7 (RFC 8312 / 9438).
   [ ] 26. Keepalive: probe an idle ESTABLISHED connection to detect a vanished peer (SO_KEEPALIVE).
   [ ] 27. SYN cookies: stateless SYN-ACK under flood; reconstruct from the returned cookie (RFC 4987).
   [ ] 28. BBR (bbr.rs): model-based control — BtlBw/RTprop filters + STARTUP/DRAIN/PROBE_BW/PROBE_RTT;
           CongestionControl becomes an enum (CUBIC or BBR); the live server runs BBR.
   [ ] 29. Multi-connection TcpServer (socket.rs): demux a 4-tuple connection table over one transport.
```

When all 29 chapters are green and clippy is clean, a stock `ping`, `nc`, and `curl` interoperate with
your stack, it survives loss/reorder under `tc netem`, and it runs both CUBIC and BBR. That is the
finish line.

## Appendix E — Further study (what this book doesn't build)

The curriculum now spans Docs 1–29 — the full lifecycle, both loss-based (NewReno → RFC 6675 → CUBIC,
Chs. 20/21/25) and model-based (BBR, Doc 28) congestion control, RACK-TLP (Doc 24), RFC 5961
robustness (Doc 23), SYN cookies (Doc 27), keepalive (Doc 26), and a multi-connection server
(Doc 29). What remains is genuinely *not built*, deliberately left as next steps (several are chapter
exercises):

- **Real rate-paced transmission** — BBR (Doc 28) computes a pacing rate but the sender is still
  window-limited; actually pacing each segment to `BtlBw` is the missing half, and only matters under
  bulk transfer the echo server never drives.
- **BBRv2 / BBRv3** — an explicit loss/ECN response and fairer coexistence with loss-based flows; Ch.
  28 builds BBRv1, which ignores loss as a signal.
- **ECN (RFC 3168)** — explicit congestion notification as a signal for either controller.
- **D-SACK (RFC 2883)** — detect spurious retransmits from duplicate SACK blocks.
- **Limited Transmit (RFC 3042)** — send new data on the first dup-ACKs to avoid an RTO on tail loss.
- **A bounded connection table + SYN-cookie fallback in `TcpServer`** (Doc 29 exercise), `0.0.0.0`
  wildcard binding, write backpressure, request bodies / chunked transfer.
- **Live conformance + load testing** — `packetdrill` against the kernel, `iperf3` under `tc netem`,
  profiling/flamegraphs (needs sudo / TUN and a live network — the one thing no offline test replaces).

None of these are missing *core*; they are breadth, alternative-version refinement, and live
validation. The core — a correct, tested, RFC-5961-hardened TCP/IP endpoint with both congestion-control
families, flood survival, and a multi-connection server — is what this book builds.
